content: Ampicillin is an antibiotic that belongs to the penicillin class of drugs. It is prescribed to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, bronchitis, and infections of the ear, lungs, skin, and urinary tract. It is important to note that antibiotics like ampicillin are ineffective against viral infections, such as colds or the flu. If you have questions about other potential uses of this medication, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Ampicillin is available in capsule form, as a liquid, and as pediatric drops for oral administration. It is typically taken every six hours (four times a day). Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Take ampicillin exactly as directed. Do not take more or less of it, or take it more frequently than prescribed. Shake the liquid and pediatric drops well before each use to ensure the medication is evenly mixed. Use the dropper provided with the bottle to measure the dose of pediatric drops. These drops or the liquid can be placed directly on a child’s tongue or mixed with formula, milk, fruit juice, water, ginger ale, or other cold liquids and consumed immediately. Capsules should be swallowed whole with a full glass of water. Continue taking ampicillin even if you feel better, and do not stop taking it without consulting your doctor. Before taking ampicillin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to ampicillin, penicillin, or any other drugs. Provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially other antibiotics, allopurinol (Lopurin), anticoagulants (blood thinners) like warfarin (Coumadin), atenolol (Tenormin), oral contraceptives, probenecid (Benemid), rifampin, sulfasalazine, and vitamins. Let your doctor know if you have or have ever had kidney or liver disease, allergies, asthma, blood disorders, colitis, stomach problems, or hay fever. Inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking ampicillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking ampicillin. Ampicillin should be taken at least one hour before or two hours after meals. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular dosing schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Ampicillin may cause side effects. Inform your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, diarrhea, vomiting, or mild skin rash. If you experience severe side effects, such as a severe skin rash, itching, hives, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, or a vaginal infection, contact your doctor immediately. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store this medication in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Capsules should be stored at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Discard any medication that is outdated or no longer needed. Liquid medication should be stored in the refrigerator, tightly closed, and any unused portion should be discarded after 14 days. Do not freeze the liquid. If kept at room temperature, the liquid is good for seven days. Consult your pharmacist about the proper disposal of unused medication. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor may order lab tests to monitor your response to ampicillin. If you have diabetes, use Clinistix or TesTape (not Clinitest) to test your urine for sugar while taking this medication. Do not share your medication with others. Your prescription is likely not refillable. If you still have symptoms of infection after completing the course of ampicillin, contact your doctor.
